chunks: I2C, SPI and UART: how each works. The question: What are the three common communication protocols? How do they (I2C, SPI, UART) work?
I2C, SPI and UART are three ways for chips on a board to pass bytes (groups of 8 bits) to each other. All three send one bit at a time, which saves wires.
They differ in how the receiver knows when to read each bit, and that choice sets their wire count, speed and how many devices they can serve.
UART links two devices with no shared clock. SPI is fast but needs a select wire per device. I2C shares two wires among many devices.
Picture three ways of passing notes in a classroom. In UART, two friends agree beforehand on how fast to talk, and each keeps their own watch.
In SPI, a teacher claps a steady beat that everyone follows, and each student has a private line to the teacher.
In I2C, the whole class shares one party line, and each student answers to their own name.
Each direction has its own wire, so both sides can talk at once.
The signal names swap (MCU TX goes to module RX) and the grounds must be common, because logic levels are voltages measured against ground.
Serial: sending bits one after another on a single wire. Clock: a steady tick on its own wire that tells the receiver when to read each bit.
Baud rate: how many bits per second both sides agreed to use. UART needs it because it has no clock wire. Chip select: a wire that wakes up one SPI device.
Address: a number that picks one device on a shared I2C bus.
Send one byte. UART adds a start bit and a stop bit, so it is 10 bits. At 115,200 baud, that is 10 over 115 200 about 86. 8 microseconds.
SPI at 8 megahertz sends the 8 bits in 8 clock ticks, which is 1 microseconds.
I2C at 100 kilohertz takes 9 ticks per byte, 8 data bits plus an acknowledge bit (the receiver's "got it"), so 90 microseconds, plus another byte for the address.
SPI is fast; I2C is slower but uses only two wires. That is the whole idea.
"UART is two wires and no clock: start bit, data LSB first, stop bit, and both sides just agree on a baud rate.
SPI is synchronous: the controller drives a clock, data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO at the same time, and each device gets its own chip-select, so it's fast but uses more pins.
I2C is two shared open-drain wires, SCL and SDA, where each device has a 7-bit address and acknowledges every byte, so it scales to many devices but runs slower, typically 100 to 400 kilohertz."
Quick check. Which of the three protocols has no clock wire between the devices?
